Guillaume Farel
gee-YOHM fah-REL
proper noun (figure)
French Guillaume — the French form of William, from the Germanic Wilhelm (wil, “will,” and helm, “helmet, protection”). The surname Farel is of Provencal origin, borne by his family in the Dauphiné region of southeastern France.

📖 Biblical Definition

Guillaume Farel (1489–1565 AD) was the fiery French evangelist and Reformer of the French-speaking Swiss lands, the man whose thundering zeal fixed the Reformation in Geneva and whose fearful adjuration compelled John Calvin to remain there. Converted under the humanist Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples, Farel forsook the errors of Rome and gave himself to itinerant, open-air preaching across Neuchatel, Lausanne, and the Vaud, overturning altars, disputing with priests, and enduring stonings, mob violence, and repeated peril of death for the gospel’s sake. He was no systematizer but a trumpet — loud, bold, tender toward Christ and terrible toward idolatry. When Calvin, then a quiet young scholar, sought only to pass a night in Geneva in 1536 on his way to a life of study, Farel sought him out and, learning of his intent, charged him in the name of Almighty God that God would curse his repose and his studies if he withheld his help from the church in her hour of need. Calvin, by his own testimony, was so stricken and terrified by this that he stayed — and the history of Reformed Geneva turned upon that word. Farel laboured on at Neuchatel to a great age, marrying late, preaching to the end, a Boanerges whose holy violence God used to plant churches that Calvin would water.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Fiery French Reformer of French-speaking Switzerland (1489–1565 AD); the evangelist of Geneva who adjured Calvin to stay.

GUILLAUME FAREL, proper noun. French Guillaume (“William”) + Farel, a Provencal surname.

French evangelist and Reformer (1489–1565 AD); converted under Lefèvre d’Étaples.

Bold itinerant preacher across Neuchatel, Lausanne, and the Vaud; endured stonings and mob violence for the gospel.

In 1536 adjured John Calvin, in the name of God, to remain in Geneva — and Calvin, terrified, stayed.

A trumpet rather than a systematizer; laboured on at Neuchatel to a great age.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of holy boldness in the preaching of the gospel.

expand to see more

Farel is sometimes reduced to a footnote in the biography of Calvin — the loud man who happened to be in the room when the great theologian was recruited. This is a diminishment born of forgetfulness rather than of any error in the man; Farel taught the sound Reformed doctrine of the grace of God in Christ, and his fault, if fault it was, lay only in a vehemence that could tip toward rashness, not in any corruption of the faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Farel recovers for a timid age is holy boldness — the readiness to preach in the open air, to overturn idols, and to bear stones and blows for the name of Christ without counting one’s life dear. His famous adjuration of Calvin teaches us that God’s call may come through a fellow labourer’s terrible earnestness, and that a man’s plans for quiet study must bow to the church’s need. Where we prize our comfort, Farel rebukes us; where we mute the gospel for peace, his trumpet still sounds.

French Guillaume (“William”) + Farel; the fiery evangelist of Geneva who compelled Calvin to stay.
